Wait: \(E_+ = -K + 2\epsilon\), so \(e^{-iE_+ t} = e^{iK t} e^{-2i\epsilon t}\). Similarly, \(e^{-iE_- t} = e^{iK t} e^{2i\epsilon t}\). So:

\[
c_{10}(t) = \frac{J}{2\epsilon} e^{iK t} \left( e^{-2i\epsilon t} - e^{2i\epsilon t} \right) = -\frac{iJ}{\epsilon} e^{iK t} \sin(2\epsilon t).
\]

\[
c_{01}(t) = \frac{J^2}{2\epsilon} e^{iK t} \left( \frac{e^{-2i\epsilon t}}{\epsilon-\Delta} + \frac{e^{2i\epsilon t}}{\epsilon+\Delta} \right) = \frac{J^2}{\epsilon} e^{iK t} \left( \frac{(\epsilon+\Delta)e^{-2i\epsilon t} + (\epsilon-\Delta)e^{2i\epsilon t}}{2(\epsilon^2-\Delta^2)} \right) = \frac{J^2}{\epsilon} e^{iK t} \frac{ \epsilon (e^{2i\epsilon t}+e^{-2i\epsilon t}) - \Delta (e^{2i\epsilon t}-e^{-2i\epsilon t}) }{2 J^2 } = e^{iK t} \frac{ \epsilon \cdot 2\cos(2\epsilon t) - \Delta \cdot 2i\sin(2\epsilon t) }{2\epsilon } = e^{iK t} \left( \cos(2\epsilon t) - i \frac{\Delta}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t) \right).
\]

Check: \(\frac{J^2}{\epsilon} \cdot \frac{1}{2(\epsilon^2-\Delta^2)} = \frac{J^2}{\epsilon} \cdot \frac{1}{2J^2} = \frac{1}{2\epsilon}\). Then numerator: \((\epsilon+\Delta)e^{-2i\epsilon t} + (\epsilon-\Delta)e^{2i\epsilon t} = \epsilon(e^{2i\epsilon t}+e^{-2i\epsilon t}) - \Delta(e^{2i\epsilon t}-e^{-2i\epsilon t}) = 2\epsilon \cos(2\epsilon t) - 2i\Delta \sin(2\epsilon t)\). Multiply by \(\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\) gives \(\cos(2\epsilon t) - i \frac{\Delta}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t)\). So yes.

Thus:

\[
c_{01}(t) = e^{iK t} \left( \cos(2\epsilon t) - i \frac{\Delta}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t) \right),
\]
\[
c_{10}(t) = -\frac{iJ}{\epsilon} e^{iK t} \sin(2\epsilon t).
\]

So the state is:

\[
|\psi(t)\rangle = e^{iK t} \left[ \left( \cos(2\epsilon t) - i \frac{\Delta}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t) \right) |01\rangle - \frac{iJ}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t) |10\rangle \right].

The overall phase \(e^{iK t}\) is irrelevant. So we can write:

\[
|\psi(t)\rangle = \left( \cos(2\epsilon t) - i \frac{\Delta}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t) \right) |01\rangle - \frac{iJ}{\epsilon} \sin(2\epsilon t) |10\rangle,
\]
up to an overall phase.

Check initial condition: at \(t=0\), we get \(|01\rangle\). Good.

So that's the exact state.

Earliest time attaining the supremum (if \(M>0\)):

If \(M>0\), then we need \(\sin^2(2\epsilon t)=1\), so \(2\epsilon t = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\)? Actually \(\sin^2\theta=1\) when \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\). So \(2\epsilon t = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\), so \(t = \frac{\pi}{4\epsilon} + \frac{n\pi}{2\epsilon}\). The earliest positive time is \(t_{\text{min}} = \frac{\pi}{4\epsilon}\), provided \(\epsilon > 0\). If \(\epsilon=0\), then \(M=0\) and it's constant, so no specific earliest time (or every time).

If \(M=0\) (constant zero), then the supremum is attained at all times.

So we can say:

If \(J=0\) (regardless of \(\Delta\)), then \(P(t)=0\) constant, so supremum 0 attained for all t.
If \(J \neq 0\), then \(M = \frac{J^2}{\Delta^2+J^2} > 0\), and earliest time is \(t = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{\Delta^2+J^2}}\), provided that \(M\) is actually attained (i.e., when \(\sin^2(2\epsilon t)=1\)). But note: If \(M<1\), it is still attained when \(\sin^2=1\). So yes, as long as \(J \neq 0\), we have \(\epsilon > 0\), and \(t = \frac{\pi}{4\epsilon}\) works.

But wait: If \(J \neq 0\) but \(\Delta\) such that \(\frac{J^2}{\epsilon^2} < 1\), it's still attained at that time because \(\sin^2(2\epsilon t)=1\) gives \(P = \frac{J^2}{\epsilon^2} = M\). So yes.

So earliest time: 
\[
t_{\text{sup}} = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{\Delta^2+J^2}} \quad \text{if } J \neq 0.
\]
If \(J=0\), then no unique earliest time (constant).
